title: Try these 5 Weave tools—and share your own
summary: Community publishing is now live for Weave tools. Here are a few tools that stand out, from turning a moodboard into a realistic room mockup to previewing your next nail set.
body_markdown:
At Config 2026, we launched[30+ custom-built Weave tools](https://www.figma.com/blog/connecting-figma-and-weave/)


[Connecting Figma and Weave Today, we’re announcing new ways your Weave creative workflows can live alongside your Figma frames.](https://www.figma.com/blog/connecting-figma-and-weave/)


in Figma to help you run repeatable image generation tasks like creating[on-brand icons](https://www.figma.com/community/weave_tool/9/on-brand-icons?q_id=d6d92143-decc-43eb-8250-3a5a7ca31bc0) or transferring a[style reference](https://www.figma.com/community/weave_tool/11/transfer-style?q_id=d6d92143-decc-43eb-8250-3a5a7ca31bc0) to a new image. As the person designing those tools, I asked myself two questions on repeat: What do designers working in Figma need, and where can[Weave’s capabilities](https://www.figma.com/blog/welcome-weavy-to-figma/)[Introducing Figma Weave: The next generation of AI-native creation at Figma](https://www.figma.com/blog/welcome-weavy-to-figma/)


[Figma has acquired](https://www.figma.com/blog/welcome-weavy-to-figma/)[Weavy](https://www.weavy.ai/) , a platform that brings generative AI and professional editing tools into the open canvas. As Figma Weave, the company will help build out image, video, animation, motion design, and VFX media generation and editing capability on the Figma platform.


meet them? The best tools don’t come from capability or need alone. They come from the intersection of the two.


Building for Figma users kept me close to that intersection, but creating tools for myself gave me the freedom to wander off. So since that first batch, I’ve built tools for my own workflows (and a few just for fun) to see how far a tool can stretch.[Professional Headshot](https://www.figma.com/community/weave_tool/92/professional-headshot) turns any photo into a new headshot,[Blue Embroidery](https://www.figma.com/community/weave_tool/110/blue-embroidery) renders a text prompt as a blue cross-stitch illustration, and[Brand Stamp](https://www.figma.com/community/weave_tool/116/wax-stamp) presses a logo into an embossed wax, chrome, or ink seal in any color.

Starting today, anyone building in[Weave](https://weave.figma.com/) can[publish tools](https://help.weavy.ai/en/articles/12267755-tools) to the Figma Community, ready to use directly on the Figma Design canvas. I believe the best way to learn how to build your own is by playing around with what other people have made. Here are some of my favorite Weave tools already published on the[Figma Community](https://www.figma.com/community/tools?tab=weave) .


## 1. Render a room from inspiration


**Created by:** Mallory Dean, Designer Advocate


**Weave tool:**[Interior Design Moodboard to Render](https://www.figma.com/community/weave_tool/100)


**What it does:** Turn an interior design moodboard into a photorealistic 3D room render. This tool reads your colors, materials, furniture, and lighting to create a cohesive space, with minimal extra styling. You can also pick from built-in room types and camera angles to guide the composition and make the space feel dynamic.


**In Mallory’s own words:** “I love using the Figma canvas to make moodboards for spaces in my home. A render workflow was the last missing step, so I built one. My biggest tip for creating Weave tools is to lean on an LLM for both parts of the job: writing your prompts and structuring your nodes. I consulted one to map out the setup that would make this tool most efficient, then as I was building, I continually brought the results back as feedback to guide my revisions.”

## 2. Transform a building photo into a realistic 3D visualization


**Created by:** Yordan Vakarelov, Building Information Modeling Manager & AI Lead


**Weave tool:**[Physical Architectural Model Maker](https://www.figma.com/community/weave_tool/107)


**What it does:** Generate an architectural model from a reference photo, with custom materials for the building, landscape, and finer details.


**In Yordan’s own words:** “I love making complex processes feel intuitive and approachable. My approach to building these workflows is to take care of the technical setup so people can focus on their creative ideas, with room to experiment and without getting bogged down in prompting or mechanics. What excites me about sharing them as tools is opening up that experience to more people and helping them build their confidence along the way. I can’t wait to see how the community takes something I’ve built, makes it their own, and creates things I’d never have imagined.”


## 3. Extend an image to fit any format


**Created by:** Jan Gericke, AI Creative Director


**Weave tool:**[Image Reframer](https://www.figma.com/community/weave_tool/94)


**What it does:** Reframe an image to any aspect ratio, to make clean space for text overlays.


**In Jan’s own words:** “Have you ever generated the perfect shot or received an image for a website header, only to realize it’s the wrong aspect ratio for where you need it? This tool is made for that exact moment. It takes your existing image and reframes it to any target ratio, extending the canvas outward while matching the original lighting, shadows, and perspective. You can tell it exactly where to place your subject in the new frame, something like ‘centered-right, keep the left quarter free,’ so it leaves clean negative space for a headline or logo. It respects the original image instead of guessing at it.”


Original 4:5 image ratio


Original image extended to a 16:9 ratio


## 4. Sketch an architectural concept from text


**Created by:** Eric Satoru, Art Director


**Weave tool:**[Sketch Generator](https://www.figma.com/community/weave_tool/97)


**What it does:** Turn a short text prompt into a hand-drawn concept sketch for an architectural project in the “what if” stage, before anything is rendered or modeled. Prompts land best when they name three things: what the space is, what it’s made of, and a view.


**In Eric’s own words:** “In a world where hyperrealistic images are easy to generate, there’s something more beautiful about using abstraction to represent an idea. AI tools usually push you straight to a polished render, which is the wrong moment for polish—a finished-looking image closes the conversation instead of opening it. I wanted something that produced rough, honest sketches at the speed of a conversation, so stakeholders could react to ideas rather than to rendering quality.”

## 5. Get a preview of your next nail set


**Created by:** Stephanie Zhou, Product Design Educator


**Weave tool:**[Nail Art](https://www.figma.com/community/weave_tool/108)


**What it does:** Personalize your dream nail set and see what it looks like on your hands before committing to it.


**In Stephanie’s own words:** “I love doing my own nails, but it can be challenging to imagine a complicated design by sketching. I wanted to get a preview of what it would look like on my own hands—and be able to make adjustments and balance the patterns—before spending 2+ hours curing everything (only to have regrets). Since this was my first Weave tool and I was designing it for myself, I started with the harder but non-negotiable features, like 3D decorations and styles. From there, I started thinking about what other people might want and where the experience could become more granular, like adding dropdowns for nail length, shape, style, and decorations. You know a project is great when you finish it with an even longer list of ideas you want to add next!”

## Ready to publish your own?


Building a tool that takes any input and returns a consistent output relies on several steps under the hood. Deciding what those steps are is the work, and once you publish, you’re making those calls for everyone who runs your tool. Three things to keep in mind:


- **Decide who you’re building for:** Before you write a single prompt, answer the question “who is this actually for?” Be specific because who you’re building for changes what your tool unlocks, exposes, and even how you label your inputs.
- **Design for the input you can’t predict:** Build a system that handles a full range of inputs without breaking—clean submissions and messy ones alike. Dropdowns and pre-made choices give people vocabulary while protecting your back end from surprises. An LLM layer between the request and the generation model can translate creative intent into something the model can work with.
- **QA like you won’t be in the room:** Give your tool to someone who didn’t build it and ask them to use it with zero explanation. Watch where they pause. Watch what they expect that doesn’t happen. Fix that before you publish.


Visit Weave’s[help center](https://help.weavy.ai/en/articles/12267755-tools) to learn more about how to build your own Weave tool. Anyone with a paid Weave plan can publish Weave tools to the Figma Community, and anyone with a full Figma seat can run Weave tools in Figma Design. Weave tools in Figma Design will consume[Figma AI credits](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/33459875669015-How-AI-credits-work) once[generally available](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/42614902212887-AI-credit-updates-FAQ) .

Her background includes photography, art direction, and creative production across gaming, marketing, media, and entertainment.
